hook.line: Tomás bursts into the café soaked and shivering. He does not need to finish the sentence: the silence tells the story better than the next clause would.

examples.en: It was raining SO hard that afternoon!

examples.es: ¡Tengo unos nervios que ni te imaginas!
examples.en: I'm so nervous you can't imagine!

rule: English finishes the job: *so cold I couldn't feel my fingers!* Spanish often stops at the big word and lets your face finish it. Three ways: *tanto* (*¡Llovía tanto!*); *un* or *una* before a feeling or weather noun (*¡Hacía un frío!*, *¡Tengo un hambre!*); *unos* or *unas* plus a noun (*¡Tenía unos nervios!*). Add *que ni te imaginas* to hand it over to the listener. Say it with a pause where the result would go.
smallPrint: Teachers call this a suspended intensifier: the consequence is cut off on purpose.

options: It rains SO much every afternoon!
It was raining SO hard that afternoon!

yourTurn.prompt: Choose *Hacía* or *Hace*: ¡___ un frío! (about yesterday). Type the whole sentence.
yourTurn.why: Yesterday is over, so the past form *hacía*.
*Tengo un hambre* and then a pause: the result is unsaid.

yourTurn.prompt: It was raining SO hard that afternoon!
yourTurn.why: *Tanto* does the intensifying, and you stop there.
*Unos* plus *nervios* is the frame for nerves.

yourTurn.prompt: Make it about we: *¡Tengo un hambre!*
yourTurn.why: Only the verb changes: *tenemos* for we.

yourTurn.prompt: Put it in the past: *¡Hace un calor!*
I'm so nervous you can't imagine! (to a friend)
yourTurn.answer: ¡Tengo unos nervios que ni te imaginas!
accept: Tengo unos nervios que ni te imaginas
yourTurn.why: *Que ni te imaginas* hands the rest to your friend.

pitfalls.why: Almost. For a story about yesterday, use the past form *hacía*.
*Hambre* is feminine but takes *un* in the singular, like *el agua*.
Here *nervios* is plural, so it matches *unos*.

personal: Think of the last time you were very cold, hungry or nervous. Write it as one hanging line, *¡Tenía un...!* or *¡Hacía un...!*, and stop there.
